★ A Scrollytelling Lesson ★

The Early
1970s
Decade Opens
Its Strange Door

Earth Day to Watergate. Smog to microchips. Five years that ended one America and started another.

▼ Begin
01 The Green Alarm

Earth Day, the EPA, and a Soundtrack That Cracked

The 1970s began with a warning that did not come from a president, a general, or a spy. It came from the rivers, the skies, the birds, the cities, and the smoke.

By 1970, many Americans had grown used to pollution as if it were weather. Some cities lived under thick . Rivers carried industrial waste. Oil spills blackened shorelines. Factories and cars helped power modern life, but they also poured chemicals into the air and water. The old American dream had promised highways, suburbs, appliances, and endless production. The new question was sharper: what happens when progress poisons the place people live?

★ The First Earth Day, April 22, 1970 ★

On April 22, 1970, the first took place. Senator helped organize it as a national on environmental problems. About 20 million Americans demonstrated in cities, towns, schools, and colleges. That was a huge number for the time. Earth Day helped push environmental protection onto the national political agenda.

Later that same year, the federal government created the , or EPA, to help enforce environmental laws and coordinate federal action on air, water, chemicals, and pollution. The EPA officially began operating in December 1970.

★ The EPA Begins Operating ★ December 1970 ★
"Smoke crossed property lines. Dirty air entered everyone's lungs."

This was a different kind of 1970s story. It was not only about soldiers, elections, or presidents. It was about people asking whether the modern world could survive its own appetite. The environment became political because smoke crossed property lines, poisoned rivers ignored city borders, and dirty air entered everyone's lungs.

An Ending in the Music, Too

The early 1970s also began with a cultural ending. In April 1970, publicly said he was no longer working with The Beatles, and the breakup became widely understood as real. The band that had helped define the 1960s was over. The dreamlike harmonies of the previous decade did not vanish, but they scattered into solo albums, lawsuits, memory, and myth.

★ John, George, Paul, Ringo ★ The Last Photo Sessions ★

So the decade opened with two signals: the planet was in trouble, and the old soundtrack had cracked.

★ Pause & Reflect

Why did pollution become a political issue in 1970?

Think before reading on. Type a quick answer below if it helps you focus.

Pollution stopped being a private inconvenience and started crossing borders. Smoke from a factory in one city blew into another. Rivers carried waste downstream past cities that did not produce it. Because the harm crossed property lines, individual choices could not fix it, so people demanded that the federal government step in. That is why Earth Day and the EPA arrived together: a public demand met a federal response.

Did it stick?

Yes, April 22, 1970. About 20 million Americans took part.
What was the EPA created to do?
Right. The EPA's job is enforcement and federal coordination.
02 New Worlds, Big and Small

Young Voters, Disney World, and a Brain on a Chip

The early 1970s were full of contradictions. The country was exhausted by war and scandal, yet it was also building new worlds.

One major political change was the , ratified in 1971. (You may have heard the mentioned in this slot, but that one was ratified in 1913 and gave Congress power to collect federal income tax.) The amendment that belongs to the early 1970s is the 26th, which lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. The argument was direct: if 18-year-olds could be drafted to fight in Vietnam, they should be allowed to vote for the leaders sending them there. The phrase often used was "old enough to fight, old enough to vote."

★ Old Enough to Fight, Old Enough to Vote ★

A Kingdom in Florida

Then came a very different kind of opening. On October 1, 1971, opened near Orlando, Florida. Disneyland in California had been surrounded by city growth. In Florida, Disney had purchased a vast amount of land, giving the company room to build not just a park, but a controlled vacation kingdom: hotels, roads, transportation systems, themed lands, and later entire additional parks.

Walt Disney had died in 1966, so he did not live to see it open. But the project carried his company's dream of engineered wonder into the 1970s.

★ Walt Disney World Opens ★ October 1, 1971 ★

A Kingdom on a Fingertip

That same year, another kingdom appeared, but it was so small it could sit on a fingertip. In 1971, Intel introduced the , often described as the first commercial single-chip microprocessor. A is like a tiny central brain for a computer: it performs calculations and follows instructions. Earlier computers could fill rooms. Microprocessors helped make smaller, cheaper, more flexible computers possible.

★ The Intel 4004 ★ A Brain You Could Lose in a Pocket ★
Democracy widened. Entertainment expanded. Computing shrank. The future was becoming portable.
★ Pause & Reflect

Three different "openings" in 1971: a constitutional amendment, a theme park, and a chip. What do they have in common?

Pause. Try to find a thread.

Each one expanded who or what could participate in modern American life. The 26th Amendment expanded who could vote. Walt Disney World expanded what a vacation could be. The 4004 expanded where computing could go. Together they signaled a country still building outward, even while war and scandal pulled inward.

The Intel 4004 was significant because it was:
Right. A central processor on a single chip, commercially sold, in 1971.
03 Diplomacy and War

Nixon in China, and the War That Would Not End Cleanly

President Richard Nixon had built much of his career as a fierce anti-communist. That made what happened in 1972 especially dramatic.

Nixon traveled to the People's Republic of China, met with and , and helped reopen relations after decades of hostility. This was called , meaning the improvement of relations between countries that had been distant or hostile.

★ Nixon and Zhou Enlai ★ Beijing, February 1972 ★

Nixon's China trip changed diplomacy because it complicated the simple picture of "communist world versus capitalist world." The Soviet Union and China were both communist states, but they had serious tensions with each other. Nixon used that division to shift global power.

Meanwhile, Vietnam Still Burned

The United States had been trying to reduce its direct role through a policy called . This meant shifting more fighting responsibility to South Vietnamese forces while withdrawing U.S. troops. Nixon wanted to end American involvement without making it look like defeat.

★ U.S. Troops in Vietnam ★

But the war had already torn American politics apart. Families argued over it. Students protested it. Veterans returned home to a country that often did not know how to honor them, understand them, or forgive itself.

★ Protest March Against the Vietnam War ★

In January 1973, the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam, and the signed the . Nixon announced that an agreement had been reached to end the war and restore peace in Vietnam. U.S. combat troops left, though the conflict inside Vietnam continued. In 1975, after the period covered here, South Vietnam fell to North Vietnam.

So when people say "the U.S. left Vietnam," they usually mean the American military withdrawal tied to the 1973 peace agreement, not the final end of the war itself.

A superpower could leave a war and still not feel free of it.

This was one of the bitter lessons of the early 1970s. Vietnam followed America home: in politics, music, movies, trauma, and distrust.

★ Pause & Reflect

Nixon was a fierce anti-communist, yet he opened relations with communist China. Why didn't this destroy his political career?

Think about who his audience was, and what made China's communism different from the Soviet Union's in 1972.

Two big reasons. First, Nixon's anti-communist record gave him credibility on the right. A liberal president might have been attacked as soft on communism for the same trip; Nixon could not be. Second, the Soviet Union and China were rivals, not partners. By opening to China, Nixon did not embrace communism, he split it. To many Americans this looked like cold strategy, not surrender, and that is how he sold it.
★ Quick Check

Did it stick?

"Vietnamization" meant:
Correct. The U.S. wanted to leave without looking defeated.
The Paris Peace Accords were signed in:
Right, January 1973. South Vietnam fell two years later, in 1975.
04 Rights, Equality, Privacy

Title IX, Roe v. Wade, and the Fight Over Rights

While foreign policy shifted, American society kept arguing over who had power, who had protection, and who had control over their own future.

In 1972, Congress passed as part of the Education Amendments. Title IX says that people cannot be excluded from, denied benefits from, or discriminated against in education programs receiving federal money on the basis of sex. In plain language: schools and colleges that take federal funds cannot treat students unfairly because they are male or female.

Title IX became especially famous for expanding opportunities for girls and women in school athletics, though its reach is broader than sports. It also affects admissions, academic programs, harassment policies, and other parts of education.

Roe v. Wade

Then, on January 22, 1973, the Supreme Court decided . The Court ruled that the Constitution protected a woman's right to choose abortion before under a right of privacy connected to the . The decision became one of the most controversial Supreme Court rulings in American history. It reshaped law, politics, religion, medicine, and elections for decades.

★ Roe v. Wade Reaches the Supreme Court ★

It is also important to know the present legal context: Roe was overturned in 2022 by , meaning abortion law is now largely decided by individual states rather than protected nationwide under Roe.

For a student, the key point is not to treat these events as simple slogans. Title IX and Roe were part of a larger struggle over equality, gender, law, education, privacy, religion, and government power. Supporters saw them as expansions of liberty and fairness. Critics, especially of Roe, saw them as legal overreach or moral wrong. These arguments did not end in the 1970s. They continued, changed shape, and remain active today.

The early 1970s were not calm after the 1960s. They were the 1960s' unfinished arguments walking into courtrooms.
★ Pause & Reflect

Title IX is famous for sports, but its actual text is broader. Why might one part of a law become more famous than the rest?

Think about visibility, measurement, and what makes a story easy to tell.

Sports are visible, countable, and televised. You can see the difference Title IX makes when a school adds a girls' soccer program or builds equal facilities. Admissions changes or harassment policies happen in offices and paperwork, with no scoreboard. So the most measurable, photographable part of Title IX became the part most people remember, even though the law applies far more widely.
★ Quick Check

Did it stick?

Title IX bans sex-based discrimination in:
Right. The federal funding link is what gives Title IX its reach.
Roe v. Wade was decided in 1973 and later overturned in 2022 by:
Correct. After Dobbs, abortion law is set largely state by state.
05 A Broken Presidency

Watergate, Resignation, and the Long Shadow

The story of the early 1970s darkened in a Washington office complex called Watergate.

★ The Watergate Complex ★ Washington, D.C. ★

On June 17, 1972, five burglars broke into the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the complex in Washington, D.C. At first, it seemed like a strange political burglary. But investigations by journalists, Congress, courts, and federal officials uncovered a wider pattern of abuse connected to President Nixon's reelection campaign and White House. The scandal was not only the break-in. It was the cover-up: the effort to hide who knew what, who ordered what, and how far responsibility went.

★ Investigative Journalism Tested Power ★

Watergate became a . That means it tested the basic structure of American government: Could a president be forced to obey the law? Could Congress investigate him? Could courts demand evidence from him? Could the press uncover wrongdoing by the most powerful office in the country?

The Tapes, the Vote, the Resignation

A key turning point came when investigators learned that Nixon had secretly recorded conversations in the White House. The Supreme Court eventually ordered him to turn over tapes. In July 1974, the House Judiciary Committee approved .

★ "Impeach Nixon" ★ Washington, D.C. ★

Facing almost certain removal, Nixon announced his resignation on August 8, 1974, and left office on August 9. He remains the only U.S. president to resign. Vice President became president.

★ Nixon Resigns ★ August 8, 1974 ★

The fall of Nixon was not just one man's tragedy. It damaged public trust in government. Coming after Vietnam, assassinations, protest, and social conflict, Watergate taught many Americans to doubt official explanations. That skepticism became part of the political culture of the 1970s and beyond.

A house with every light on, and a president walking away from power before power could remove him.

So the early 1970s close like a house with every light still on: Earth Day in the streets, young voters at the polls, Disney gates opening, microchips humming, diplomats crossing into China, soldiers leaving Vietnam, women and students fighting for rights, and a president walking away from power before power could remove him.

The decade did not begin quietly. It began with endings, inventions, exposures, and the uneasy feeling that America had entered adulthood the hard way.

★ Pause & Reflect

Why is Watergate often called a constitutional crisis instead of just a scandal?

What was actually being tested?

A scandal is embarrassing personal misconduct. Watergate tested whether the Constitution's structure still worked. Could Congress investigate a president? Could the courts force him to hand over evidence? Could the press break stories the White House wanted buried? If any of those failed, presidential power would have grown beyond the Constitution's reach. They held, barely, and Nixon resigned. That is why "constitutional crisis" is the right phrase.
